title: How METR measures Long Tasks and Experienced Open Source Dev Productivity - Joel Becker, METR
talk_summary: Joel Becker presents METR's RCT finding that experienced open-source developers were ~19% slower when allowed to use AI (Cursor), despite believing they were faster, and discusses why AI struggles on mature repos with high tacit context.

takeaways.technique: Self-reported speedup is unreliable; measure actual task time
takeaways.what_they_do: METR randomized real issues to AI-allowed vs AI-disallowed and measured actual completion time rather than asking developers, finding self-reports inverted the sign of the effect.
takeaways.evidence_quote: developers will tell you that they were faster when they weren't
takeaways.numbers: ~19% slowdown measured vs developers predicting ~1.5x speedup; 16 developers

takeaways.technique: AI output needs expensive human cleanup on high-context codebases
takeaways.what_they_do: Observed that AI makes directional progress but misses project conventions and correctness, so experts spend costly time verifying and cleaning up; novices can't do that cleanup at all.
takeaways.evidence_quote: the humans not only need to spend expensive time verifying, but also like clean up clean up all the stuff

takeaways.technique: Tacit repo context is the bottleneck, not raw coding
takeaways.what_they_do: Argues AI fails on mature repos because conventions and implicit knowledge aren't written down; experts hold mental context the model lacks.

takeaways.technique: Scope tasks down to fit model capability
takeaways.what_they_do: Notes that models fail on large, fuzzy tasks and succeed when problems are scoped smaller and shaped like benchmarks.
takeaways.evidence_quote: at first I would try problems that were too large and like it can't handle that

takeaways.technique: Fuzzy real-world goals expose agent failure modes
takeaways.what_they_do: Cites AI Village where agents given underspecified real goals (organize event, run store) fail badly, suggesting qualitative observation of where they break.
takeaways.evidence_quote: basically all the time they find that the models fall on their faces and suck
